questions.question: Which set lists characteristics used to define living things?
options: Movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion, nutrition
questions.rationale: The classic checklist — MRS GREN — describes life by processes: Movement, Respiration, Sensitivity, Growth, Reproduction, Excretion, Nutrition.

questions.question: Why are viruses generally classified as non-living?
options: They are too small to see
They lack their own metabolism and cannot move or respond
They never reproduce in any way
questions.rationale: Viruses reproduce and evolve only inside host cells and have no independent metabolism, movement, or response — failing most of the checklist.

questions.question: A candle flame moves, 'grows', consumes fuel, and produces waste, yet is not alive because:
options: It lacks internal organisation, reproduction, and response driven from within
questions.rationale: Life requires organised internal processes; a flame's behaviour comes purely from outside fuel and convection physics.

questions.question: The sum of all chemical reactions inside an organism is called:
questions.rationale: Metabolism includes anabolic (building) and catabolic (breaking down) reactions powering every characteristic of life.

questions.question: A heart can beat though no single muscle cell can. This illustrates:
options: Emergent properties at higher levels of organisation
That organs violate the characteristics of life
questions.rationale: New properties appear as levels stack: cells contract, but the beating emerges only at the organ level.

questions.question: Mimosa leaves folding when touched is an example of which characteristic of life?
questions.rationale: Sensitivity means responding to the environment — the Mimosa folds its leaves when touched.

questions.question: Kidneys filtering urea from the blood illustrate which characteristic?
questions.rationale: Excretion is removing metabolic waste, and the kidneys filtering urea is the lesson's example.

questions.question: A mule cannot produce fertile offspring yet is still considered alive. Why?
options: Because reproduction counts at the level of the species, not the individual
questions.rationale: The lesson explains that a mule's sterility doesn't disqualify it: reproduction is judged for the species, not every individual.

questions.question: Which sequence shows biological levels in increasing order of complexity?
options: Cell -> Tissue -> Organ -> Organ system -> Organism
questions.rationale: The hierarchy stacks up from cell to tissue to organ to organ system and finally organism.

questions.question: According to the lesson, which single trait is by itself enough to declare something living?
options: None — life requires organised processes working together
questions.rationale: No single trait — movement, growth, even reproduction — is sufficient; life is defined by processes in a bounded, self-maintaining system.
